articles.title: How to Pass an Enterprise AI Security Review: Build an Evidence Pack That Closes Deals
articles.excerpt: Your demo went well. The buyer's team is excited. Then the deal moves to security review, a questionnaire arrives with dozens of AI-specific questions, and the momentum stops. Weeks pass. Someone asks…
articles.body: Your demo went well. The buyer's team is excited. Then the deal moves to security review, a questionnaire arrives with dozens of AI-specific questions, and the momentum stops. Weeks pass. Someone asks whether your agent logs are tamper-proof. Someone else asks how you would reconstruct a wrong decision for a regulator. Your best answer is a paragraph of reassurance. This is where many vertical AI deals are won or lost, and it is a problem you can prepare for. This guide shows how to build an evidence pack: a small, standing set of artifacts that answers the AI-specific questions with records instead of promises. It covers what reviews now ask, the five questions that decide most of them, the pack itself, how to run a live replay in the buyer meeting, and a two week plan to get it done.
articles.author: Mir Arshad Ali Talpur

articles.title: A Step-by-Step Guide to fMRI Registration with FSL and ANTs

articles.body: This tutorial explains how to register functional MRI data to a participant's T1-weighted anatomical image and then to an MNI template. Each step introduces the required inputs, the command to run, its outputs, and how to inspect the result. We use FSL's boundary-based EPI registration and ANTs' nonlinear anatomical registration. This tutorial presents one workflow combining the two tools. Processing runs from a Linux terminal; visual inspection uses FSLeyes in a graphical desktop session. My earlier article, Installing FSL and FIX on Linux , covers the FSL setup. ANTs must also be installed and available on your PATH ; see the ANTs installation guide . Scope: The examples follow the linked official documentation and use generic filenames.
articles.author: Haruki Niwa

articles.title: How to archive YouTube videos in TypeScript without relying on saved URLs
articles.excerpt: Saving a download URL doesn't finish your archive. Your overnight job finishes, and you save download_url for next week's processing queue. It feels settled. Then you notice expires_at. Signed S3/R2 l…
articles.body: Saving a download URL doesn't finish your archive. Your overnight job finishes, and you save download_url for next week's processing queue. It feels settled. Then you notice expires_at . Signed S3/R2 links last 1–7 days, independently of the object's storage lifecycle. An expired link doesn't prove the archived file is gone. It proves your saved permission to fetch it has expired. Choose storage for the worker that arrives later A signed URL carries temporary authorization. An object key identifies what you want. Your archive needs both concepts, even when the first download works. This recipe uses a private S3 bucket and a narrow input schema for that route.

articles.title: Running a Local LLM Chat on Android: Apps, Termux, and What to Expect
articles.excerpt: I wanted to chat with a language model on my phone without shipping every message to someone's server. It turned out I did not need root, a flagship device, or a cloud account - just enough free stora…
articles.body: I wanted to chat with a language model on my phone without shipping every message to someone's server. It turned out I did not need root, a flagship device, or a cloud account - just enough free storage and a bit of patience. Here is what I learned while trying the different ways to get an LLM running locally on Android. What a local AI companion actually is A local companion is simply an app that runs the language model on the phone itself instead of calling a remote API. The model is the neural network that writes the replies. Because it lives on your device, the conversation stays there and keeps working in airplane mode. Most of these apps support model families such as Gemma, Llama, Phi or Mistral.

articles.title: Flight Starlink Prediction: What Probabilistic Availability APIs Teach About Agent Data Sourcing
articles.excerpt: A flight Starlink prediction tool hit Hacker News with 276 points and 362 comments. The tool estimates whether your flight will have working satellite internet based on flight number, date, and aircra…
articles.body: A flight Starlink prediction tool hit Hacker News with 276 points and 362 comments. The tool estimates whether your flight will have working satellite internet based on flight number, date, and aircraft assignment. It does not give binary answers. It surfaces likelihood scores when data is incomplete. This is a useful case study for agent data sourcing. The problem space has no official API, partial rollouts, time-sensitive equipment assignments, and a user expectation of confidence intervals instead of yes/no flags. The plumbing exposes how agents handle probabilistic infrastructure predictions when ground truth arrives days late. The Data Model: Three-Tier Lookup The tool runs a cascading filter: Airline check : Does this carrier have Starlink at all? If not, return 0% immediately.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
articles.excerpt: "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon. Everyone is very confident on this."
articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.
